findings.title: uploadStatus's 503 'retry, not terminal' payload is unreachable to the app's own client, so the poll loop treats a transient storage hiccup as a terminal failure -- the opposite of the documented intent
findings.detail: controllers.py:419-444 introduces a 503 response for uploadStatus carrying {"error", "state": "running", "terminal": false, "job"} specifically so the client keeps polling instead of ending the loop (docstring at controllers.py:420-424 and the inline comment at controllers.py:433 both say this explicitly). But api/client.js's shared handle() (client.js:80-86) throws an ApiError for ANY response.status outside 200-299 before the body is ever parsed for its structured fields -- it only extracts a plain 'error' string via readErrorDetail() for the user-facing message; 'state'/'terminal'/'job' are discarded. The ApiError it throws does not carry the parsed body either (no `body` passed to the constructor in that branch). In ngiab-upload-run.js's _await() poll loop, the catch block at lines 133-138 treats any thrown error as terminal: it calls this._busy(false) and returns, ending the loop and showing an error message. So when uploadStatus answers 503, the app's own reference frontend stops polling and reports the upload as failed -- exactly the behavior the backend change was written to prevent. A non-browser consumer written against the documented 200-only convention and using the common 'raise_for_status() then read body' idiom will hit the identical trap.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) have uploadStatus answer this case with 200 plus terminal:false so the existing success path in client.js delivers the body unchanged, or (b) make client.js's handle() attach the parsed JSON body to the thrown ApiError for non-ok responses (when parseable), and change ngiab-upload-run.js's catch block at line 135 to inspect error.status === 503 / error.body?.terminal === false and `continue` the poll loop instead of returning. Also cross-reference: components/ngiab-upload-run.js:116-145.

findings.title: ingest.read_status can synthesize a 'failed' state that was never written by the job, with no field marking it as synthetic -- a race can cause the client to report failure on a run that later succeeds
findings.detail: ingest._fail_if_stale (ingest.py:133-159), invoked from read_status (ingest.py:130), rewrites the returned document's state to FAILED and fabricates a message when `updated` is older than STALE_AFTER_SECONDS (default 30 min), even though the on-disk status document the ingest process actually wrote is untouched. The synthesized document is indistinguishable from a genuinely-written failure (no 'synthetic' or 'stale' marker), so any consumer that treats state=='failed' as authoritative -- including the shipped poll loop, which stops polling on any terminal state (ngiab-upload-run.js:141) -- will report failure and never learn if the underlying process was merely slow and later wrote DONE. Unlike the 60-minute POLL_CEILING_MS backstop in the frontend, which tells the user to reload and check, this earlier (30 min default) server-side failure carries no such caveat in its message, so the user is told the run failed with no hint that it might still appear.
findings.suggested_fix: Mark the synthesized document distinctly (e.g. a `synthetic: true` or `stale: true` field) so consumers and future maintainers can tell it apart from a writer-recorded failure, and phrase the message to acknowledge the run may still complete/appear (mirroring the POLL_CEILING_MS message), rather than asserting 'Nothing was published.'

findings.title: New env vars controlling ingest concurrency and staleness are not documented in README.md
findings.detail: NGIAB_MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS (controllers.py, MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS default 2), NGIAB_UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY (ingest.py, default 16), and NGIAB_JOB_STALE_SECONDS (ingest.py, STALE_AFTER_SECONDS default 30*60) all change observable API behavior (503 'busy' responses, failure timing) but do not appear in README.md or the frontend README.md. Operators deploying this app have no documented way to discover or tune these knobs, and API consumers have no documented explanation for the new 503 'uploads are already being prepared' failure mode.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short section to README.md documenting NGIAB_MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS, NGIAB_UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY, and NGIAB_JOB_STALE_SECONDS, including their defaults and the new 503/failure behaviors they produce.

residual_risks: startUpload/uploadRun now returning 503 ({error}, MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS reached) and 500 ({error}, launch failed) instead of always 200 {job,state} is not itself a broken contract -- the failure is distinguishable from success purely via HTTP status code, which client.js's handle() already branches on before body inspection, and the previous behavior on launch failure was an unhandled exception (an opaque 500 with no JSON body at all), so this is a net improvement for any consumer that already treats non-2xx as failure generically. Low confidence this needs action; flagged only for completeness.

The _upload_directory concurrent-upload/cleanup rewrite in ingest.py (partial-run cleanup via run_store._delete_prefix, manifest-last ordering) changes internal reliability characteristics but does not alter the public HTTP contract of uploadRun/startUpload/uploadStatus; not flagged as a contract issue.
testing_gaps: No test appears to exercise uploadStatus's 503 branch end-to-end through the actual frontend (api/client.js + ngiab-upload-run.js) to confirm the poll loop keeps polling rather than terminating -- the code inspection above shows it currently does not.
No test appears to cover ingest._fail_if_stale racing against a job that writes a terminal DONE status shortly after being read as stale-failed.
No test appears to cover _start_or_report's IngestBusy path end-to-end (that discard_staged is actually called and the presigned-upload object is removed when MAX_CONCURRENT_INGESTS is hit).
